nodes.description: GlialCAM is the obligatory subunit that brings MLC1 out of the endoplasmic reticulum to astrocyte-astrocyte junctions and stabilizes it, and it also targets the ClC-2 chloride channel to junctions and changes its gating. Without GlialCAM, MLC1 accumulates intracellularly and is lost from the plasma membrane; in Glialcam-null mouse astrocytes MLC1 expression is abolished and ClC-2 reduced. Patient missense GlialCAM variants still modify ClC-2 currents in vitro but no longer place the channel at junctions. Knockout of either gene, or of both, gives the same phenotype in mice and zebrafish, so GlialCAM and MLC1 act as one functional unit.

Recessive variants tested so far do not reduce binding to MLC1 or ClC-2, so the defect is one of location rather than of partner binding.

nodes.description: A function of GlialCAM outside the MLC1 complex. Conditional deletion of Hepacam from developing mouse astrocytes reduces astrocyte territory and morphological complexity, impairs gap junction coupling between astrocytes and shifts the balance between synaptic excitation and inhibition. In the germline Glialcam-null mouse, astrocyte gap junction coupling is only modestly reduced and the syncytium stays electrically isopotential. Whether the recessive patient alleles impair coupling has not been tested.

nodes.description: Reduced GlialCAM in astrocytes leaves MLC1 off the membrane, impairs activation of the volume-regulated anion current (VRAC, carried by LRRC8 channels) and increases vacuolation, as MLC1 loss does. Co-expressing GlialCAM with mutant MLC1 restores VRAC currents. In acute brain slices from Glialcam-null mice, cortical astrocytes recover volume less well after potassium-induced swelling, so the defect is not an artefact of culture. The link from the MLC1-GlialCAM complex to LRRC8 appears indirect, through signalling rather than physical association.
